finds.lens: Oscillators and mean reversion (B_/S_rsi14, bb_pctB, consec_down/up_days, is_20d_low, is_63d_low) — oracle distributions vs the daily_panel denominator, with the reverse conditional P(oracle buy | oversold) as the primary discriminator.

findings.claim: Oversold is a modest-precision, low-recall marker of oracle buys: 29.8% of all RSI<30 days became an oracle buy, but only 15% of oracle buys were RSI<30.
findings.stat: P(oracle buy | rsi14<30) = 25/84 = 29.8% of daily_panel days. Recall = 25/167 unique buy-days = 15.0%. RSI<25: 13/37 = 35.1% precision, 7.8% recall. Full window Jan-2023–Aug-2026, both indices, nothing dropped.
findings.base_rate: P(any daily_panel day is an oracle buy-day) = 167/1817 = 9.19%. Only 4.6% of all days are RSI<30 (84/1817).
findings.why_not_tautology: Precision is the honest direction of the conditional and it is only 3.2x — 70% of oversold days were NOT oracle buys, and 85% of oracle buys were not oversold. The lift itself is largely tautological (see the stratified test below): a month's best entry is by construction near a local price low, and RSI is a monotone function of recent price. What separates them is the forward-return test, reported as a separate finding.

findings.claim: The non-tautological version survives: measured on ALL daily_panel days with no oracle selection, RSI<30 days had ~3x the base forward 5-day return, and it held in every one of the four calendar years.
findings.stat: Forward 5d return from close: RSI<25 mean +2.04% (n=37, 81% positive); RSI 25-30 mean +1.64% (n=47, 66% positive); RSI 30-40 +0.88% (n=202). By year, RSI<30 5d mean: 2023 +1.74%, 2024 +1.98%, 2025 +1.67%, 2026 +2.31%. Forward returns computed from the panel's own close series; 10 rows lost at h=5, 42 at h=21 (end of panel).
findings.base_rate: All days: 5d mean +0.48% (n=1807), median +0.57%, 61% positive. 10d mean +0.94%; 21d +1.90%.
findings.lift: +1.20pp to +1.56pp excess 5d mean, i.e. 3.4x–4.3x the unconditional mean; +20pp on hit rate (81% vs 61%) at RSI<25
findings.why_not_tautology: This statistic never touches the oracle trade list. The denominator is every day in daily_panel and the numerator is realised forward price, so selection-on-outcome cannot generate it. The real caveat is different and is not selection: the 84 RSI<30 days collapse to 14 independent episodes (gap>5 days) across two highly correlated indices — 2023-09/10, 2025-03, 2025-04, 2026-03 dominate. Effective n is closer to 14 than 84, and every one of those episodes sits inside a bull market that recovered.

findings.claim: RSI adds almost nothing once you already know the price is at a 20-day low — the oscillator is mostly a re-encoding of 'price is locally low', which is Rule 3 in its purest form.
findings.stat: Among is_20d_low days: with rsi14<30, P(buy)=24/59=40.7%; with rsi14>=30, P(buy)=26/80=32.5%. The oscillator's marginal contribution inside the local-low stratum is +8.2pp (1.25x relative), against a raw standalone RSI<30 lift of 3.24x. In the deeper drawdown stratum (dd_from_20d_high < -5%), rsi<35 gives 0.227 vs rsi>=35 0.130 — a real but smaller 1.75x residual.
findings.base_rate: is_20d_low alone: 50/139 = 36.0% (lift 3.91x) vs the 9.19% all-day base. Only 7.6% of all days are 20-day lows.
findings.lift: Standalone RSI<30 lift 3.24x collapses to 1.25x once conditioned on is_20d_low
findings.why_not_tautology: It IS mostly the tautology, and that is the finding. is_20d_low is the stronger and simpler variable (3.91x vs 3.24x) and it absorbs most of RSI's apparent edge. The small residual in the deep-drawdown stratum (1.75x) is the only part that could be oscillator-specific, and n there is 188 days / far fewer episodes.

findings.claim: The oracle buys the month's price low, not the month's oscillator low — 91% of index-months had the lowest-low day as an oracle buy versus 55% for the lowest-RSI day.
findings.stat: Across 88 sym-month groups (44 months x 2 indices): the day with the month's minimum intraday low was an oracle buy in 80/88 = 90.9% of months; the day with the month's minimum rsi14 was an oracle buy in 48/88 = 54.5%. Mean within-month RSI percentile rank of oracle buy days = 0.301 (0 = lowest RSI in the month).
findings.base_rate: With 2 buys per index-month out of ~21 trading days, a randomly chosen day is a buy ~9.5% of the time; so the 'random' expectation for either extreme day is ~9.5%.
findings.lift: Price-low 9.6x vs random; RSI-low 5.7x vs random — but the RSI-low day is only 60% as likely to be the buy as the price-low day
findings.why_not_tautology: The price-low number is near-mechanical: the oracle fills at the intraday low and maximises the month's summed return, so it is nearly forced to take the month's cheapest bar. That 90.9% is the tautology quantified. The useful content is the 36-point GAP: if RSI were a sufficient statistic for 'cheap', the two numbers would coincide. They do not, so RSI-lowest and price-lowest are different days about 40% of the time, and the oracle picks price.

findings.claim: The buy-side relationship is a smooth gradient, not a threshold: there is no RSI level below which the lift jumps. The only genuine cliff is on the overbought side.
findings.base_rate: 9.19% unconditional; the flat middle (RSI 40–75) spans 1,072 days and never departs more than 25% from base
findings.lift: Monotone-ish 1.1x→3.8x descending from RSI 45 to RSI 20; a single discontinuity from 0.80x to 0.14x at RSI 75
findings.why_not_tautology: The gradient shape is the useful part regardless of tautology — it says no threshold rule is being rewarded and any 'RSI<30' cut point is an arbitrary slice of a continuum. The [30,35) inversion is the multiple-comparisons warning made visible: with 12 bins tested, one inverted bin is expected. Do not read the 3.82x on n=37 as a discovered threshold.

findings.claim: The overbought exclusion is near-absolute for oracle buys yet has zero forward-return content — it is the cleanest pure tautology in this lens.
findings.stat: rsi14>75 OR bb_pctB>1.0 OR consec_up_days>=5 covers 389 days (21.4% of the panel) and contains only 4 of 167 oracle buy-days (P=1.03%, lift 0.11x), missing just 2.4% of buys. consec_up_days>=5: 114 days, ZERO buys. But the same 389 days' forward returns are fine: 5d mean +0.34% (60% positive) and 21d mean +2.14% (77% positive).
findings.base_rate: 9.19% buy rate; all-day forward 5d +0.48%/61% positive and 21d +1.90%/71% positive
findings.lift: 0.11x on oracle-buy probability, but 1.13x on forward 21d mean return (i.e. the exclusion zone outperformed on realised price)
findings.why_not_tautology: Explicitly high and I am not defending it. The oracle needs a subsequent higher high inside the same calendar month; a day already at a 5-day-up-streak extreme is by construction not the cheapest bar of its month, so it cannot be a buy. The forward-return column proves the point: those days went UP more than average over 21 days. Anyone converting 'the oracle never buys overbought' into 'do not buy overbought' would be trading a construction artefact against the actual data.

findings.claim: The sell side is far weaker than the buy side, and overbought oscillators do not mark tops: the best sell discriminator is only 2.2x, and RSI>70 days had ABOVE-average forward returns.
findings.stat: P(oracle sell | condition) vs 9.52% sell base: is_20d_high 97/461 = 21.0% (2.21x, 56% recall); is_63d_high 20.4% (2.15x); rsi>80 15.0% (1.58x, n=133, 12% recall); rsi>75 14.0% (1.47x); bb_pctB>0.95 12.3% (1.29x). 27% of oracle sells happened at RSI<50; median sell RSI is 62.9. Forward returns on RSI>70 days: 10d mean +1.05%, 75% positive; 21d +1.93%, 76% positive.
findings.base_rate: P(any day is an oracle sell-day) = 173/1817 = 9.52%. Compare buy-side best: is_20d_low 3.91x, rsi<25 3.82x.
findings.lift: Best sell lift 2.21x vs best buy lift 3.91x — a 43% weaker signal; and RSI>70 forward 10d +1.05% vs base +0.94% (1.12x, i.e. no reversal)
findings.why_not_tautology: The oracle-sell asymmetry is partly structural (a sell must be at a local high the same way a buy must be at a local low), so 2.21x vs 3.91x is a statement about the oracle. But the forward-return leg is selection-free and is the load-bearing half: on 403 overbought days measured against realised price, there is no mean reversion at all — momentum, if anything. 'Sell the overbought print' has no support here even though oracle sells cluster at highs.

findings.claim: Deeper oversold is WORSE, not better: is_63d_low underperforms is_20d_low both as an oracle marker and, more importantly, on selection-free forward returns, where it is the only oversold condition that loses to the base rate.
findings.stat: is_63d_low: 16/54 = 29.6% oracle-buy rate (lift 3.22x, 9.6% recall) vs is_20d_low 50/139 = 36.0% (3.91x, 29.9% recall). Forward returns on is_63d_low days: 5d mean +0.40%, MEDIAN -0.14%, only 48% positive; 21d median +0.85%. is_20d_low: 5d +0.63%/58% positive. Contrast bb_pctB<0.05 (n=130): 5d +1.14%, 21d +3.42%.
findings.base_rate: All days 5d mean +0.48%, median +0.57%, 61% positive; oracle-buy base 9.19%
findings.lift: Forward 5d median -0.14% vs +0.57% base = -0.71pp, and 48% vs 61% hit rate (0.79x); oracle lift 3.22x vs 3.91x for the shallower flag
findings.why_not_tautology: The forward-return half never touches the oracle list. The 54 days collapse to 10 episodes concentrated in 2025-03, 2026-03, 2023-09/10 — small and clustered, so confidence is weak — but the direction is consistent with the oracle side (fewer 63d-lows become buys than 20d-lows) and with a mechanism: a 63-day low means the 20-day-scale bounce has already failed, so the trend is still down when the oracle's one-month window forces an exit.

dead_ends: Combining oscillators does not beat the single best variable. rsi<35 AND bb_pctB<0.1 gives P(buy)=29.4% (n=109, 3.19x) and bb<0.05 AND is_20d_low gives 31.6% (n=98, 3.44x) — both BELOW is_20d_low alone at 36.0% (3.91x). Every two-way combination I tried traded recall for no precision gain.

bb_pctB has no threshold structure below the band. P(buy) is 26.2% at bb<0.05, 26.2% at bb<0.10, 22.9% at bb<0.20 — flat across the whole lower tail. The apparent 'below the lower band' (bb<0) special case (29.5%, n=88) is within noise of bb<0.30 (19.2%, n=344) scaled by the gradient.

Per-index robustness is a wash and offers no story: SPX is_20d_low 4.26x vs NDX 3.55x, but SPX rsi<30 2.70x vs NDX 3.74x — the ranking of which index the oscillator works better on flips between variables, which is what noise at n=40-70 per cell looks like.

consec_down_days looked like a clean ladder (>=2 2.26x, >=3 2.97x, >=4 3.63x, >=5 4.35x) but the top rungs are tiny: >=5 is 15 days total, 6 buys. The ladder is the same 'price is low' gradient in another coordinate — it is 97 unique dates across 54 episodes and adds nothing on top of dd_from_20d_high.

No level of RSI cleanly separates oracle sells. 27% of oracle sells occurred at RSI<50 and the minimum sell RSI is 22.2 — i.e. the oracle repeatedly sold into weakness because the calendar-month boundary forced the exit. The month boundary, not the oscillator, is what ends these trades.

I could not test whether oversold readings coincided with macro events (FOMC, CPI, NFP) because the panel has no event calendar — BRIEF.md flags this. The 14 RSI<30 episodes look event-clustered (2025-03, 2025-04, 2026-03) but I have no way to attribute them and did not.

finds.lens: CALENDAR AND TIMING — where in the month, week and year oracle buy/sell dates fall, benchmarked against (a) the daily_panel base rate and (b) a purpose-built "shifted-box" null that re-runs the exact oracle optimiser on 21-day windows offset from the calendar month. Scripts: /home/user/INMA-/research-vault/backtest/scratch/{cal2..cal8,box,box2}.py. Nothing dropped: all 176 trades, all 44 months, both symbols used everywhere. Aug-2026 is a partial month (13 trading days) and is included, as it is in the oracle. Panel is 907 spx + 910 ndx rows (a 3-day mismatch I did not reconcile).

findings.claim: Oracle buys cluster on the first two trading days of the calendar month far beyond what month-boxing alone explains — this is the only calendar effect in the dataset with genuine calendar content.
findings.stat: 56/176 buys (31.8%) fall on trading-day 1 or 2 of the month. Identical in SPX (28/88, 31.8%) and NDX (28/88, 31.8%); by year 27.1% / 31.2% / 33.3% / 37.5% (2023-26). Trading-day-1 alone: 38/176 = 21.6%.
findings.base_rate: daily_panel: 176/1817 days = 9.69% are trading-day 1-2 of a month (tday=1 is 88/1817 = 4.84%). Order-statistic null (20,000 draws of 4 ordered days per sym-month, matching each month's day count): 15.2% for buys.
findings.lift: 3.28x vs panel base rate; 2.09x vs the order-statistic null; 1.30x vs the shifted-box null (24.4%), z=+1.93, empirical p=0.047 (only 1 of 42 offset windows reached 31.8%).
findings.why_not_tautology: I rebuilt the oracle exactly (O(T) DP reproduces all 88/88 sym-month solutions, verified date-for-date) and re-ran it on windows of identical length offset by every k in ±1..21 trading days. An arbitrary 21-day box picks its own first two days 24.4% of the time — that is the pure argmin-at-the-edge artifact of boxing a trending price path, and it has zero calendar meaning. The CALENDAR month's first two days get picked 31.8%, at the very top of the 42-offset distribution. The excess is calendar-specific and matches the documented turn-of-month inflow anomaly. Selection-on-outcome is weak here because no months were selected: the oracle runs on all 44/44 months for both symbols, so there is no month-level survivorship — only within-month selection, which is exactly what the shifted-box null neutralises. Caveat: z=+1.93 with 62 hypotheses examined in this lens, and effective n is ~110 not 176 (see SPX/NDX co-timing finding).

findings.claim: The mirror-image 'sell window' at month-end is ENTIRELY a boxing artifact and has no calendar content whatsoever — it is the finding in this lens that looks most spectacular and is most certainly fake.
findings.stat: 55/176 sells (31.2%) land on the last two trading days of the month; leg-2 sells alone are 53/88 = 60.2%. Raw lift over panel looks like 3.22x (aggregate) / 6.22x (leg2).
findings.base_rate: daily_panel: 176/1817 = 9.69% of days are in the last two trading days of a month. Shifted-box null (oracle re-run on 42 offset 21-day windows): 30.0% of all sells and 57.5% of leg-2 sells land in the last two days of the window.
findings.lift: 3.22x vs panel; 1.04x vs the shifted-box null (z=+0.30, empirical p=0.37 — 15 of 42 offset windows scored HIGHER than the real calendar). Leg-2: 6.22x vs panel but 1.05x vs box null (p=0.37).
findings.why_not_tautology: It IS the tautology. Any within-window maximiser puts its final sell at the window edge when the path trends up, and offsetting the window by 7, 8, or -13 trading days produces 74.4%, 75.6%, 72.1% — higher than the real calendar's 60.2%. Report this as a debunked effect, not a finding. It matters because the naive panel comparison (3.2x, n=176) would have passed rules 1 and 2 unchallenged.

findings.claim: Every leg1-vs-leg2 timing difference is 100% mechanical and carries zero information — the optimiser constraint buy1<=sell1<=buy2<=sell2 forces it.
findings.stat: Median trading-day-in-month: leg1 buy = 2.0, leg1 sell = 8.5, leg2 buy = 13.0, leg2 sell = 19.5. Leg-1 buys land in the last two days of a month 0/88 times; leg-2 sells land in the first two days 1/88. Leg-1 buys at start-of-month TOM: 50/88 (56.8%); leg-2 sells at end-of-month TOM: 53/88 (60.2%).
findings.base_rate: daily_panel: start-TOM 176/1817 = 9.69%, end-TOM 176/1817 = 9.69%, mid-month 1465/1817 = 80.63%. The order-statistic null reproduces the entire leg1/leg2 ordering pattern by construction.
findings.lift: 5.87x (leg1 buy at start-TOM) and 6.22x (leg2 sell at end-TOM) vs panel — both fully absorbed by the ordering constraint plus the box-edge artifact. Lift vs shifted-box null: 1.26x and 1.05x.
findings.why_not_tautology: Nothing separates them. The two legs are ordered by definition, so 'leg1 is earlier' is a restatement of the spec. I include it so nobody reports it as a discovery. The only residue worth anything is the leg-1 buy at 56.8% vs shifted-box 45.3% (empirical p=0.093), which is the same turn-of-month signal already reported in finding 1 and is not independent evidence.

findings.claim: Options expiry has no independent timing content: days_to_opex is a near-monotone reparameterisation of trading-day-in-month, and the oracle holds through opex week at exactly the base rate.
findings.stat: Of 1,227 trade-holding days (buy date through sell date inclusive, both indices), 401 are opex week = 32.7%. Buys avoid opex week (39/176 = 22.2%) and sells avoid it (44/176 = 25.0%), but leg-1 SELLS are enriched (38/88 = 43.2%) and leg-2 BUYS are enriched (32/88 = 36.4%) — i.e. opex week is simply the mid-month leg-1-out/leg-2-in swap point.
findings.base_rate: daily_panel: 581/1817 = 31.98% of days are opex week; is_opex_week=1 spans days_to_opex in [-4,+4] calendar days.
findings.lift: Holding days: 1.02x (32.7% vs 31.98%). Buys 0.69x vs panel but 0.72x vs the order-statistic null — i.e. the depression is 100% explained by 'oracle buys are not mid-month', nothing to do with expiry. Largest raw days_to_opex cell (dto=+15, 22 buys, 3.15x vs panel) collapses to 2.14x against the position null and is just trading-day 1-3.
findings.why_not_tautology: It is positional, not expiry-related. The clean test — is the oracle disproportionately IN or OUT of the market during opex week — returns 1.02x on n=1,227 holding days. Flat. Report as a dead end. NOTE: there is no event calendar in this data (BRIEF known gaps), so opex is the only scheduled event testable at all; FOMC/CPI/NFP proximity cannot be evaluated.

findings.claim: There is no month-of-year, year, or quarter-end seasonality in oracle opportunity; monthly opportunity is a volatility function, not a calendar function.
findings.stat: Mean oracle month_total_pct by calendar month (n=6-8 sym-months each): Jan 10.04, Feb 7.98, Mar 9.39, Apr 14.49, May 10.69, Jun 9.59, Jul 7.28, Aug 10.13, Sep 8.47, Oct 8.31, Nov 10.65, Dec 7.57 — total spread 7.3-14.5 on n<=8. By year: 9.41 / 9.32 / 10.67 / 8.83 (2023/24/25/26, n=24/24/24/16). Quarter-end months 8.86 (n=28) vs other months 9.98 (n=60). Correlation of month_total_pct with mean realvol20 across the 88 sym-months: +0.835; with ATR14%: +0.800; with that month's buy&hold return: only +0.372.
findings.base_rate: daily_panel monthly buy&hold: mean +1.92%, sd 4.13, range -5.79 to +13.97 across the same 88 sym-months. Trade COUNTS by month and year are fixed at 4 per month by construction (44 months x 2 legs x 2 symbols), so no frequency test on calendar month is even possible — only magnitude.
findings.lift: Month-of-year spread (7.3-14.5, sd across the 12 month-means = 2.0) is small against within-cell sd 4.21 with n<=8 per cell (se ~1.5). Quarter-end 8.86 vs 9.98 = 0.89x on n=28/60. Volatility, by contrast, has r=+0.835 (R^2=0.70).
findings.why_not_tautology: This is a null result and negatives are not vulnerable to selection-on-outcome in the same way. The one substantive positive here — oracle opportunity tracks realised vol at r=+0.835 while tracking the month's actual direction at only +0.372 — is itself somewhat tautological (a wider intraday range mechanically permits a bigger low-to-high capture), and I flag it as such. April's 14.49 mean rests on n=8 sym-months and includes the April-2025 tariff shock; do not read it as seasonality.

findings.claim: The apparent day-of-week signal (buy Monday, sell Thursday/Friday) does not survive removing turn-of-month days or checking year-by-year stability.
findings.stat: Raw: buys Mon 41/176 (23.3%), Tue 25 (14.2%); sells Thu 46 (26.1%), Fri 41 (23.3%), Mon 26, Tue 27. Net buys-minus-sells by weekday: Mon +15, Tue -2, Wed +2, Thu -9, Fri -6. EXCLUDING turn-of-month days: buy-Mon lift falls to 0.92 (19/111), sell-Thu to 1.15 (25/110). Sell-on-Thu-or-Fri share by year: 62.5% (2023) -> 52.1% -> 43.8% -> 34.4% (2026), monotonically decaying to below the 39.9% base rate.
findings.base_rate: daily_panel weekday shares: Mon 342/1817 = 18.82%, Tue 20.75%, Wed 20.53%, Thu 19.92%, Fri 19.98%. Thu+Fri = 39.90%. Excluding turn-of-month days (n=1465): Mon 18.6%, Tue 20.4%, Wed 21.2%, Thu 19.8%, Fri 20.1%. The order-statistic null is ~identical to the panel for weekday (buy-Mon 20.06%), confirming weekday is orthogonal to within-month position.
findings.lift: Headline 1.24x (buy Mon) and 1.31x (sell Thu); ex-turn-of-month 0.92x and 1.15x. Effect sizes are ~2 sd at best (buy-Tue deficit 25 vs 36.5 expected, sd 5.4) across 10 buy + 10 sell weekday cells tested.
findings.why_not_tautology: Weekday is the one calendar axis genuinely orthogonal to the month-boxing artifact, so it deserved a real look — and it fails on its own terms. The residual buy-Tuesday deficit (0.66x ex-TOM, 15/111) is the only cell still standing, and at -1.8 sd out of 20 cells I treat it as noise. Report as a dead end, not a weekend effect.

findings.claim: Effective sample size is roughly 110, not 176: SPX and NDX pick the SAME buy date in 81% of sym-month-legs, so every calendar statistic above is near-duplicated and its error bars are understated.
findings.stat: Across the 88 (month, leg) pairs: identical buy_date in 71 (80.7%), identical sell_date in 57 (64.8%); within 1 calendar day, 73 buys and 68 sells. Consequently every calendar distribution is near-identical by symbol — buys in first-2-trading-days: SPX 28/88 (31.8%), NDX 28/88 (31.8%); sells at end-TOM: SPX 31.8%, NDX 30.7%; buy-opex-week SPX 22.7% vs NDX 21.6%.
findings.base_rate: daily_panel contains 907 spx + 910 ndx rows over the same 44 months — the panel treats them as 1,817 independent day-observations, which is the same over-counting on the denominator side.
findings.lift: n/a — this is a variance correction, not an effect. Multiply reported standard errors by roughly sqrt(176/110) = 1.26.
findings.why_not_tautology: Direct measurement of date agreement, independent of outcome selection. The practical consequence: my finding-1 z of +1.93 becomes ~+1.5 on the deduplicated sample, which moves it from marginal to suggestive. I have NOT re-run the shifted-box null on a deduplicated basis. Also worth stating plainly: there is no SPX-vs-NDX calendar difference to report — the two indices are the same trade 81% of the time.

findings.claim: Zero of 176 oracle buys fall on trading-day 10 of the month, and only 1 on trading-day 16 — this is exactly the kind of spectacular-looking cell that 23-way binning manufactures, and it should not be reported as a finding.
findings.stat: tday=10: 0 buys observed, 8.5 expected (4.84% of 176). tday=16: 1 buy, 8.5 expected. tday=6: 2 buys. Raw lifts: 0.00x, 0.12x, 0.23x.
findings.base_rate: daily_panel: each of trading-days 1-13 is exactly 88/1817 = 4.84% of days; the order-statistic null gives 4.89% for tday=10 buys, i.e. the position constraint does not depress it at all.
findings.lift: 0.00x — apparently infinite, actually meaningless.
findings.why_not_tautology: Not a tautology, just a multiple-comparisons artifact. With 176 draws spread over 23 tday cells, P(a given mid-month cell is empty) = (1-0.0484)^176 = 0.02, and across ~20 eligible cells the expected number of empty cells is ~0.4 — so seeing one is unremarkable. I include it as the explicit example of rule 2 in action, and to pre-empt anyone else mining the same column.

dead_ends: Day-of-week: died once turn-of-month days were excluded (buy-Mon 1.24x -> 0.92x, sell-Thu 1.31x -> 1.15x) and showed monotone year-over-year decay in sell-Thu/Fri (62.5% -> 34.4%). Weekday is orthogonal to the month-boxing artifact, so this was the cleanest available test and it returned nothing.

Opex proximity: days_to_opex is a monotone restatement of trading-day-in-month; holding-day coverage of opex week is 32.7% vs a 31.98% base rate (lift 1.02, n=1,227 holding days). No expiry effect at entry, exit, or during the hold.

Quarter-end months: oracle month_total 8.86 (n=28 sym-months) vs 9.98 (n=60) — a 0.89x lift that tracks the same direction as buy&hold (1.27 vs 2.22), i.e. lower-vol quarters, not a quarter-end effect.

Month-of-year and year-of-sample seasonality: trade COUNTS are fixed at 4 per month by construction so no frequency test exists; on magnitude, the 12 month-means span 7.3-14.5 on n<=8 each against a within-cell sd of 4.21, and the four year-means span 8.8-10.7. Nothing.
Calendar-day-of-month (B_dom / S_dom) and tdays_in_month: entirely redundant with tday_in_month once month length is controlled; added no information beyond the trading-day axis.

Same-day (hold=0) trades, n=23: checked weekday (Thu 9, Mon 4, Wed 4, Fri 4, Tue 2), turn-of-month (13/23), opex week (4/23), leg (16 leg1 / 7 leg2) and symbol (14 spx / 9 ndx). Every cell is <=13 observations; with n=23 split across 5-23 bins nothing here is interpretable and I make no claim from it.

finds.lens: TREND AND STRUCTURE — where oracle buys sit vs the 20/50/200DMA, drawdown depth from 20d/63d/252d highs, and run-up from lows, bucketed by month-level regime. All numbers from oracle_features.csv (176 trades, none dropped) against daily_panel.csv (1,817 days, none dropped except where noted for forward-return construction).

findings.claim: Oracle buys are shallow pullbacks inside an uptrend, not correction lows: 87.5% of buys are ABOVE the 200DMA and the median buy is only 3.87% below its 252-day high.
findings.stat: 176 buys: median B_dist_sma200 +7.04% (Q25 +3.12, Q75 +9.82); median B_dd_from_252d_high -3.87%; 12.5% of buys below the 200DMA; 14.2% deeper than -10% from the 252d high; 6.8% deeper than -15%. Jan-2023 to Aug-2026, SPX+NDX.
findings.base_rate: daily_panel 1,817 days: median dist_sma200 +8.89%, median dd_from_252d_high -1.94%; 9.2% of days below the 200DMA; 11.9% deeper than -10%; 5.4% deeper than -15%.
findings.why_not_tautology: The DEPTH half is tautological (an oracle buys price lows, so it sits below recent highs by construction). The load-bearing half is the opposite direction and survives: selection-on-outcome should drag buys toward deep lows if that is where the biggest rallies start, and it barely does — the lift on every 'real correction' threshold is 1.2-1.35x, versus 2.0-2.6x on 20-day-horizon thresholds. The perfect-foresight trader in this window was overwhelmingly buying shallow dips in an intact uptrend because that is what the window contained.

findings.claim: The apparent 'the oracle prefers short-horizon dips to deep drawdowns' gradient is an artifact of the backtest's monthly constraint, not a market fact: each feature's lift is bounded by its WITHIN-MONTH share of variance, and the two rank-orders match almost exactly.
findings.stat: Lift on buys: dist_sma20<0 1.97x, dist_sma50<0 1.76x, dist_sma200<0 1.35x; dd20<-5% 2.14x, dd63<-5% 1.71x, dd252<-10% 1.19x. Within-sym-month share of total variance (panel, 88 sym-months): dist_sma20 51.4%, dist_sma50 23.7%, dist_sma200 12.5%; dd_from_20d_high 44.4%, dd_from_63d_high 23.4%, dd_from_252d_high 9.9%.
findings.base_rate: 1,817 panel days decomposed into 88 sym-months; within-month SD is ~1.6-2.0 for every one of these features while total SD ranges 2.38 to 5.57 — the long-horizon features barely move inside a single month.
findings.lift: Rank correlation between the six lifts and the six within-month variance shares is perfect (both order sma20 > sma50 > sma200 and dd20 > dd63 > dd252); lift ratio 1.97/1.35 = 1.46x against variance-share ratio 51.4/12.5 = 4.1x.
findings.why_not_tautology: This is a statement about the estimator, not about the trades. The oracle is FORCED to take 2 buys in every calendar month, so it has zero cross-month regime selection — it can only move a feature by as much as that feature moves within a month. Any 'the oracle avoids deep drawdowns' or 'the oracle likes the 200DMA' reading of this dataset is reading the rule that generated it. This kills, rather than supports, the naive trend findings.

findings.claim: Every trend/structure feature at the buy date is the SAME finding — 'the oracle buys the month's price low' — and none carries incremental information: within-month percentile rank is 0.21-0.28 for all of them, and ~1 buy in 3 is the exact monthly extreme of each feature.
findings.stat: Mean within-sym-month percentile of the buy-date value (0 = lowest day that month): dd_from_20d_high 0.215, dist_sma50 0.222, dd_from_252d_high 0.219, dist_sma200 0.226, dd_from_63d_high 0.226, dist_sma20 0.229, up_from_20d_low 0.268, rsi14 0.277. Share that is the month's minimum: 29.5-39.8%. Leg 2 is more extreme than leg 1 (dd20 percentile 0.174 vs 0.255).
findings.base_rate: A day picked at random inside its own sym-month has expected percentile 0.500 and is the month's minimum with probability 1/20.4 = 4.9% (mean 20.4 trading days per sym-month).
findings.lift: 0.22 vs 0.50 expected = -0.28 in percentile units; monthly-minimum hit rate ~32% vs 4.9% = 6.5x.
findings.why_not_tautology: This IS the tautology, measured rather than avoided. Reported because it sets the ceiling for every other claim in this lens: because all eight features collapse to the same within-month rank, a multi-feature 'trend filter' built from this dataset would be one feature counted eight times. What would separate them is a control that fixes the price rank and asks which local low was bought — done in the next finding, where the discrimination turns out to be ~1.1x, i.e. essentially none.

findings.claim: Given a dip, the oracle does NOT discriminate uptrend dips from downtrend dips — it takes whatever the month offers, so 'buy the dip only above the 200DMA' gets no support from this dataset.
findings.stat: Among the 74 oracle buys with B_dd_from_20d_high < -3%, 75.7% were above the 200DMA (median B_dist_sma200 +4.37%).
findings.base_rate: Among ALL 404 panel days with dd_from_20d_high < -3%, 68.8% were above the 200DMA (median dist_sma200 +3.44%).
findings.lift: 75.7% vs 68.8% = 1.10x (a 6.9pp difference on n=74, i.e. ~5 trades).
findings.why_not_tautology: Both sets are conditioned on being a dip, so the 'oracle buys lows' tautology is held fixed on both sides of the comparison. What is left is a genuine choice the oracle could have expressed and did not. Note this is the one place a trend filter COULD have shown up in oracle behaviour, and it is flat — which is itself constrained by finding 2 (the oracle cannot skip a month it dislikes).

findings.claim: Bucketing the 44 months (88 sym-months) by how deep the market went that month: the oracle's per-trade payoff roughly doubles from shallow to deep months, but the buy's position vs the 200DMA is set by the regime, not chosen within it.
findings.stat: By month minimum dd_from_252d_high — A shallow >-3% (27 sym-months, 54 trades): median trade +3.61%, median B_dd252 -1.40%, median B_dist_sma200 +8.95%, 0.0% of buys below 200DMA, median hold 7d. B mild -3..-7% (28 mo, 56 tr): +3.93%, 3.6% below 200DMA. C correction -7..-15% (25 mo, 50 tr): +4.56%, median B_dist_sma200 +3.60%, 20.0% below 200DMA, median hold 3d. D deep <-15% (8 mo, 16 tr): median trade +7.31%, median B_dd252 -18.39%, 62.5% below 200DMA. Median month sum-of-legs 7.55% / 8.20% / 10.04% / 14.00%.
findings.base_rate: Panel days in the same four buckets (548 / 576 / 527 / 166 days): share of days below the 200DMA 0.0% / 0.7% / 15.7% / 48.8%; median dd_from_252d_high -0.27 / -1.78 / -5.26 / -16.59.
findings.lift: Buys below 200DMA vs same-bucket base rate: bucket C 20.0% vs 15.7% = 1.27x, bucket D 62.5% vs 48.8% = 1.28x — i.e. after conditioning on the month, the oracle's 200DMA 'preference' shrinks from 1.35x to ~1.28x and is worth ~1 trade in bucket D. Payoff lift deep vs shallow = 7.31/3.61 = 2.02x per trade, 14.00/7.55 = 1.85x per month.
findings.why_not_tautology: The payoff-by-depth result is largely a VOLATILITY restatement, not a drawdown one: median realised 20d vol runs 19.4 / 16.1 / 13.8 / 11.1 across depth quartiles of the same months, so a perfect-foresight trader mechanically harvests more where the bars are bigger. The non-tautological residual is the 1.27-1.28x within-bucket 200DMA lift, which is small enough to be sampling noise on 16 and 50 trades. Bucket D rests on 8 sym-months (Jan/Feb/Mar-2023 NDX, Jan-2023 SPX, Apr-2025 both) — 4 calendar episodes, not 8 independent ones.

findings.claim: The structure-to-forward-upside relationship is real in the DENOMINATOR, independent of the oracle: on all panel days, the 10-day maximum achievable upside is ~2.6x larger below the 200DMA than above it, and ~2.4x larger deep in a 252-day drawdown than near the high.
findings.stat: Forward panel built from close and high (1,797 days; the last 10 trading days of each index dropped for lack of lookahead — 20 rows). Median (max high over next 10 sessions / close - 1): ALL days 2.19%; above 200DMA 2.05% (n=1,629); below 200DMA 5.38% (n=168). By dd_from_252d_high: >-3% 1.86% (n=1,077); -7..-3% 2.41% (n=384); -15..-7% 3.71% (n=237); <-15% 4.37% (n=99). Median forward 5d close-to-close: 0.52% above 200DMA vs 2.17% below.
findings.base_rate: The all-days median of 2.19% (10d max-upside) and 0.58% (5d close-to-close) IS the base rate; each bucket is quoted against it.
findings.lift: below/above 200DMA = 5.38/2.05 = 2.62x on max-upside, 2.17/0.52 = 4.2x on 5d close return; dd252<-15% vs >-3% = 4.37/1.86 = 2.35x.
findings.why_not_tautology: This measurement never touches the oracle's trade selection — it is every day in the window, so selection-on-outcome cannot produce it. The real weakness is different and larger: the 168 below-200DMA days are not 168 independent observations. They fall in 19 runs that collapse to about 5 macro episodes (Jan-Mar 2023, Oct-Nov 2023, Mar-May 2025, Mar-Apr 2026), and the two 2025/2026 episodes dominate. Effective n is ~5, not 168. AS A RULE this would read 'below the 200DMA, 10-day upside roughly doubles' — the out-of-sample test is the identical computation on 2010-2022 SPX/NDX and on non-US indices, and IT HAS NOT BEEN RUN. It is also not tradeable as stated: the metric exits at an intraday high nobody can hit.

findings.claim: The oracle's buy side is structurally far more extreme than its sell side — buys sit near the monthly floor, sells only modestly above the middle — so in this dataset the trend/structure information is concentrated almost entirely at entry.
findings.stat: Mean within-sym-month percentile: B_dist_sma20 0.229 vs S_dist_sma20 0.588; B_dd_from_20d_high 0.215 vs S 0.591; B_dist_sma200 0.226 vs S 0.661. Flags: 30.7% of buys are on a 20-day low, 9.7% on a 63-day low; 56.8% of sells are on a 20-day high, 43.8% on a 63-day high. 59.1% of buys are below the 20DMA vs 22.2% of sells.
findings.base_rate: Panel: 7.6% of all days are a 20-day low, 25.4% a 20-day high, 3.0% a 63-day low, 19.9% a 63-day high; 30.0% of days sit below the 20DMA. Random-day within-month percentile = 0.500.
findings.lift: is_20d_low: 30.7% vs 7.6% = 4.01x at the buy; is_20d_high: 56.8% vs 25.4% = 2.24x at the sell. In percentile terms the buy deviates -0.28 from random while the sell deviates only +0.09 (dist_sma20), a ~3x asymmetry.
findings.why_not_tautology: Both sides are selected on outcome, so extremity at both ends is expected; the claim here is only about the RELATIVE size, and part of that is mechanical — the leg-1 sell must precede the leg-2 buy, so it cannot be the month's high. That split is visible: leg-1 sells rank 0.53-0.57 within month while leg-2 sells rank 0.61-0.65, while leg-2 buys rank 0.174-0.195 versus leg-1 buys at 0.255-0.264. What would separate a real asymmetry from the sequencing constraint is re-running the oracle with a single unconstrained pair per month and re-measuring both percentiles; not done.

findings.claim: Within the oracle, how deep the buy was barely predicts how big the trade was — the regime the month was in matters roughly 3x more than the individual entry's structure.
findings.stat: Trades sorted into quartiles by buy-date feature (n=44 each): B_dd_from_252d_high Q1 (deepest) median return 5.06% vs Q4 3.62%; B_dd_from_20d_high 4.67% vs 4.06%; B_dist_sma200 4.67% vs 4.01%; B_dist_sma20 4.34% vs 4.17%; B_rsi14 4.18% vs 4.06%.
findings.base_rate: All-oracle median trade return 4.05%; median 10-day max achievable upside on a random panel day is 2.19% (the non-oracle reference for what a 5-day-median hold can capture).
findings.lift: Deepest-vs-shallowest quartile spread: 5.06/3.62 = 1.40x for dd252, and 1.15x or less for the other four features. Compare the cross-month regime spread of 7.31/3.61 = 2.02x (finding 5).
findings.why_not_tautology: Every trade in the comparison is oracle-selected, so the level of returns is meaningless; only the ORDERING across quartiles is being read, and the ordering is nearly flat. The direction of the bias here works against the claim — if entry structure mattered, selection-on-outcome would amplify the gradient, not flatten it. Confounded with volatility: deep-drawdown buys occur in high-realised-vol months (19.4 vs 11.1 annualised across depth quartiles), so even the modest 1.40x is plausibly all vol.

dead_ends: dist_sma200 as an INDEPENDENT selector: its within-sym-month percentile at the buy (0.226) is statistically indistinguishable from dd_from_20d_high (0.215) and dist_sma20 (0.229). Inside a month the 200DMA barely moves, so 'distance from the 200DMA' is just 'price rank in the month' wearing a different name. No incremental information over any other structure feature.

up_from_252d_low_pct and up_from_63d_low_pct: buys sit at median 28.48% / 7.43% above the 252d/63d low versus base rates of 31.02% / 9.88% — lifts of 0.92x and 0.75x, indistinguishable from the mechanical consequence of buying a low. The 'run-up from lows' family added nothing the drawdown family did not already say.

Below-the-200DMA months as an oracle-selection story: only 5 of 88 sym-months have a median dist_sma200 <= 0 (ndx 2023-01, ndx/spx 2025-03, ndx/spx 2025-04), covering 104 of 1,817 panel days and 10 of 176 trades. Their headline numbers look dramatic (median trade +8.77%, 90% of buys below the 200DMA) but the same-bucket base rate is 90.4% of days below the 200DMA — lift 1.00x. Zero signal, pure regime composition.

Buy-date trend structure as a predictor of trade size: five features tested by quartile (dd252, dd20, dist_sma200, dist_sma20, rsi14); four of the five have a quartile spread under 0.7 percentage points on a ~4% median return. Reported as finding 8 precisely because it is a null.

'below 200DMA AND not currently dipping' showing the highest forward 10d upside in the panel (6.51% median, vs 4.27% for below-200 dips): n=42 days, and inspection of the run structure shows they are the post-low recovery legs of the Mar-May-2025 and Mar-Apr-2026 episodes. One or two episodes wearing a bucket label; discarded rather than reported.

Same-day (hold=0) trades as a distinct structural regime: 23 of 176 per the brief. Their buy-date trend features track the full sample closely enough that no separate trend/structure statement survived, so no split is reported here — flagged because same-day legs use the same bar's low and high and would distort any hold-length-vs-structure claim.

finds.lens:
RATES AND MACRO — does the yield backdrop or the yield impulse mark oracle buys?

SCOPE AND WHAT I DROPPED (rule 5). Nothing was capped or sampled: all 176 trades, all 1,817 panel rows, all 44 months, all 4 years. Two disclosures. (a) DEDUPLICATION: every macro column (ust_*, curve_*, dxy, tlt, hyg, gold, wti and their 5d changes) is IDENTICAL for spx and ndx on the same date — I verified 0 of 910 dates disagree on ust_y10. So the panel's macro denominator is 910 unique dates, not 1,817 rows, and the 176 trades collapse to only 98 unique BUY dates and 115 unique SELL dates. Every base rate and lift below is computed on that deduplicated basis; using 1,817/176 would double-count each observation and halve the honest standard error. I report trade-level n where it differs. (b) MISSINGNESS: ust_*_chg5d is null on 6 of 910 panel dates and 2 of 98 buy dates (Treasury curve forward-fill gap per the brief's known-gaps note), so yield-impulse tests run at n=904 panel / n=96 buys / n=174 trades. All other macro columns are complete.

HOW MANY THINGS I TESTED (rule 2). 22 distinct macro columns (7 tenors, 2 curve slopes, 3 yield 5d-changes, 5 asset levels, 5 asset 5d-changes), each examined at buy dates and sell dates, under ~6 framings apiece (level, median, sign of change, mean magnitude, absolute magnitude, tail threshold), and each cut 5 ways by year (2023 / 2024 / 2025 / 2026 / all). That is on the order of 140 distinct comparisons before the 3 decontamination conditionings. At that count some 1.5x lift is guaranteed by chance. My defence is not a p-value: it is that the one finding I promote is monotone in its threshold, stable across all 4 years, and survives conditioning on three separate confounders. The dozen things that did NOT survive are listed as dead ends, and they are the majority.

2026 IS A PARTIAL YEAR: Jan-19 Aug 2026, 158 panel dates and 32 trades (14 unique buy dates). Its per-year lifts are the noisiest in every table.

HEADLINE. The yield DIRECTION is a clean null and the yield IMPULSE MAGNITUDE is the signal. Oracle buys are not marked by falling yields, rising yields, a steeper curve, a flatter curve, or any yield level — they are marked by the 10Y and 30Y having MOVED A LOT in either direction in the prior 5 sessions. The mean signed 10Y 5d change at buys (+0.6bp) is statistically indistinguishable from the base rate (+0.7bp) while the mean absolute change is 29% larger (13.2bp vs 10.2bp). This is a dispersion effect with zero directional content, which is what makes it interesting: the obvious tautology ("rallies start when rates fall") predicts a directional shift and there is none.

CREDIT (HYG) LOOKS STRONG AND IS NOT. HYG falling into a buy shows the single largest raw lift in the whole lens (1.42x, consistent all 4 years) and mirrors perfectly at sells. It is the textbook rule-3 tautology and I killed it: conditioning on the equity's own 5d return collapses the lift to 1.01-1.14, and the HYG move orthogonalised to SPX (beta 0.264, n=907) shows buys at 53.1% negative vs a 50.9% base rate — nothing. HYG does not lead. It co-moves. I report it as a negative because it is the most seductive number here.

RULE 4. Nothing below is a strategy. "Buy when |10Y 5d change| >= 15bp" fires on 25.6% of all days (233 of 910) and the oracle only takes 98 of them, so the rule as stated has a ~10% precision ceiling against a 10.8% unconditional base — it is a filter that removes 74% of the calendar, not an entry. The out-of-sample test I have NOT run: fix the threshold on 2023-2024, then on 2025-2026 measure forward 5/10/20-day returns of a fixed-horizon long entered on shock days versus all days, with the same yield data vintage and no look-ahead in the 5d window. Also unrun and necessary: 2015-2022, where the rate-vol regime was entirely different and this effect may not exist at all.

NO EVENT CALENDAR (brief's known gap). The obvious mechanism for a clustered 10Y move is FOMC/CPI/NFP, and I cannot test that — those dates are not in the data. The finding should be read as "large rate repricing precedes oracle lows" with the driver unidentified, not as an FOMC claim.

findings.claim: Oracle buys cluster on days following a LARGE 10Y move in either direction: 41.7% of buy dates had |10Y 5d change| >= 15bp versus 25.6% of all days, and the effect is present in all four years.
findings.stat: |ust_y10_chg5d| >= 15bp on 41.7% of unique oracle buy dates (40/96) over Jan-2023 to Aug-2026. Mean absolute 5d 10Y move at buys 13.2bp vs 10.2bp base (+29%). Per year (buy% vs panel%, lift): 2023 69.2% vs 40.6% (1.71, n=26); 2024 45.2% vs 30.6% (1.48, n=31); 2025 20.0% vs 15.6% (1.28, n=25); 2026-partial 21.4% vs 10.1% (2.12, n=14). Monotone in threshold: >=5bp lift 1.13, >=10bp 1.24, >=15bp 1.63, >=20bp 1.82, >=25bp 2.11, >=30bp 2.02. Trade-level (n=174, both indices) 40.2%.
findings.base_rate: 25.6% of all 904 non-null panel dates have |ust_y10_chg5d| >= 15bp (231/904). Base rate by year: 2023 40.6% (n=244), 2024 30.6% (n=252), 2025 15.6% (n=250), 2026 10.1% (n=158) — the base rate itself collapses fourfold as rate vol normalises, which is why the per-year comparison is mandatory and the pooled number alone would be misleading.
findings.lift: 1.63x pooled (41.7% vs 25.6%, +16.1pp absolute). Range 1.28x-2.12x across the four years; positive in every year.
findings.why_not_tautology: Three independent decontaminations. (1) SIGN IS DEAD: mean signed 10Y 5d change at buys is +0.6bp vs +0.7bp base rate — identical. A directional 'rates fell so stocks rallied' tautology predicts a shift in the mean and there is none; only the second moment moves. (2) NOT VOLATILITY REGIME: conditioning on SPX realvol20 tercile gives lift 1.62 / 1.65 / 1.61 (low/mid/high, panel n=302/301/298) — flat across the entire vol distribution, so this is not 'oracle buys happen in high-vol regimes and rate vol tracks equity vol'. VIX-percentile terciles give 2.25 / 1.25 / 1.54, strongest in the LOWEST VIX tercile, the opposite of what the vol-regime confound predicts. (3) NOT THE EQUITY SELLOFF: conditioning on SPX 5d return, the lift is 0.96 in the <-2% bucket (n=29 buys) but 1.85 in -2..0% (n=35) and 2.06 in 0..+2% (n=26) — the rate shock is most distinctive precisely among buys that did NOT follow a big equity drop, which is where the equity-drawdown tautology has no purchase. REMAINING RISK, named honestly: rate-shock days have 21% wider intraday ranges (median 1.005% vs 0.832%), and the oracle fills at the INTRADAY LOW, so a wider bar is mechanically likelier to contain the month's best price. Conditioning on intraday-range tercile shrinks but does not remove the lift: 2.75 (buy n=11), 1.48 (n=25), 1.27 (n=60). Read the honest effect as ~1.3-1.5x, not 1.63x. Also: shock-buys do NOT earn more (median oracle ret 3.93%, n=70, vs 4.21% for calm-buys, n=104), so the shock marks WHERE the low sits, not how large the rally is — consistent with a location effect rather than a return effect.

findings.claim: A FALLING 10Y in the 5 days into a buy is NOT more common than base rate — the directional yield impulse carries essentially zero information about oracle buy timing, and its sign flips year to year.
findings.stat: ust_y10_chg5d < 0 on 46.9% of unique oracle buy dates (45/96) vs 45.1% of panel dates. Median 10Y 5d change at buys +1.0bp, identical to the panel median +1.0bp. By year (buy% vs panel%, lift): 2023 57.7% vs 45.1% (1.28, n=26); 2024 35.5% vs 43.3% (0.82, n=31); 2025 56.0% vs 51.6% (1.09, n=25); 2026 35.7% vs 38.0% (0.94, n=14). Two of four years point the wrong way. Same null for 2Y (52.1% vs 47.1%, lift 1.11, n=96) and 30Y (40.6% vs 44.5%, lift 0.91).
findings.lift: 1.04x pooled (+1.8pp). Per-year lifts 1.28 / 0.82 / 1.09 / 0.94 — straddling 1.0 with no consistent sign.
findings.why_not_tautology: This is a measured null, and a null cannot be a selection artifact — selection on outcome would, if anything, manufacture a directional yield signal, and it did not. It is also the answer to the lens question as literally posed. The regime context explains why: the panel correlation between SPX 5d return and 10Y 5d change is -0.352 in 2023, -0.165 in 2024, +0.179 in 2025 (SIGN FLIP — 2025 was a growth-scare regime where falling yields meant bad news for equities), -0.348 in 2026. A directional rate rule that worked in the 2023 hiking regime would have been inverted in 2025. The one caveat: this is a null at the 5-day horizon on par-curve data forward-filled to the last business day; a 1-day or intraday yield impulse is untestable here and could differ.

findings.claim: HYG falling into a buy is the largest raw effect in this lens (1.42x, all four years) and it is a tautology — it vanishes once you condition on the equity's own 5-day move. Credit does not lead; it co-moves.
findings.stat: hyg_chg5d < 0 on 65.3% of unique oracle buy dates (64/98) vs 45.9% base; trade-level 65.9% (n=176). Mirror at sells: 33.0% (n=115). By year (buy% vs panel%, lift): 2023 53.6% vs 46.8% (1.14, n=28); 2024 74.2% vs 44.8% (1.65, n=31); 2025 68.0% vs 43.6% (1.56, n=25); 2026 64.3% vs 50.0% (1.29, n=14). KILL TEST: conditioning on SPX 5d-return bucket, buy% vs panel% becomes 86.2 vs 85.1 (lift 1.01, buy n=29), 77.8 vs 69.8 (1.11, n=36), 40.7 vs 35.9 (1.14, n=27). Regressing HYG 5d %change on SPX 5d return over the panel (beta=0.264, alpha=-0.058, n=907) and taking residuals: buys are 53.1% negative vs a 50.9% panel base rate (lift 1.04), median residual -0.042% vs -0.022% panel. Residual by year, buy vs panel: 50.0/51.2 (2023), 51.6/51.6 (2024), 52.0/45.6 (2025), 64.3/58.1 (2026) — nothing anywhere.
findings.base_rate: 45.9% of 910 panel dates have hyg_chg5d < 0. Residual-basis base rate: 50.9% of 907 panel dates have a negative SPX-orthogonalised HYG 5d move.
findings.lift: 1.42x raw (65.3% vs 45.9%, +19.4pp) — collapses to 1.01-1.14x within equity-return buckets and 1.04x on the orthogonalised residual.
findings.why_not_tautology: It IS the tautology, and I am reporting it as a negative precisely because it is the most seductive number in the lens. HYG is a credit ETF whose 5d return loads on equities at beta 0.264; oracle buys are selected because a rally followed, i.e. they sit at local equity lows; so 'HYG was down into the buy' restates 'the equity was down into the buy'. What WOULD separate them: a residual HYG move materially more negative at buys than at equity-matched panel days — measured above and it is not (53.1% vs 50.9%). One thin thread survives on the SELL side: median residual at sells is +0.110% vs -0.022% panel, with only 17.5% of sells in the panel's bottom residual quartile vs 24.9% expected (n=114). That is a modest credit-outperformance tilt at oracle tops, but it rests on a linear beta fit that may mis-specify HYG's convexity in stress, and I would not promote it without a nonlinear control.

findings.claim: The sell side is the mirror image: oracle sells land in CALM rate conditions, and the asymmetry is sharpest in 2026 where not one sell date followed a 15bp+ 10Y move.
findings.stat: |ust_y10_chg5d| >= 15bp on 21.7% of unique sell dates (25/115) vs 25.6% base — lift 0.85, against 1.63 at buys. By year (sell% vs panel%, lift): 2023 27.6% vs 40.6% (0.68, n=29); 2024 30.6% vs 30.6% (1.00, n=36); 2025 19.4% vs 15.6% (1.24, n=31); 2026 0.0% vs 10.3% (0.00, n=19). Mean absolute 10Y 5d move at sells 9.8bp vs 10.2bp base and 13.2bp at buys.
findings.base_rate: 25.6% of 901 non-null panel dates; per-year 40.6% / 30.6% / 15.6% / 10.3%.
findings.lift: 0.85x at sells vs 1.63x at buys — a 1.9x buy/sell ratio in rate-shock incidence.
findings.why_not_tautology: Sells are selected on outcome too (they are the intraday highs that maximise the month's summed return), so this is not a free result. But the asymmetry is informative in a way neither leg alone is: if rate shock were merely a proxy for 'volatile period' it would elevate BOTH legs, since buy and sell of the same 5-day trade sit in the same regime — median hold is only 5-5.5 trading days, so the two legs share most of their 5d yield window. Instead buys are 1.63x and sells 0.85x. The remaining confound is the same intraday-range mechanism as finding 1 operating in reverse. The 2026 0.0% is on n=19 sell dates in a partial year against a 10.3% base — expected count is ~2, so this is entirely consistent with chance and should not be read as a regime statement.

findings.claim: The rate-shock effect lives at the LONG end: 30Y shows it (1.57x), 2Y essentially does not (1.18x) — so this is term-premium/duration repricing, not a Fed-path repricing.
findings.stat: |5d change| >= 15bp at unique buy dates vs panel: ust_y30 33.3% vs 21.2% (lift 1.57, n=96); ust_y10 41.7% vs 25.6% (1.63); ust_y2 31.2% vs 26.5% (1.18). Signed means at buys are again flat: 2Y -2.1bp vs -0.1bp panel, 10Y +0.6 vs +0.7, 30Y +1.4 vs +1.0.
findings.base_rate: Panel |5d change| >= 15bp: ust_y2 26.5%, ust_y10 25.6%, ust_y30 21.2% (n=904 each).
findings.lift: 30Y 1.57x, 10Y 1.63x, 2Y 1.18x. The 2Y lift is ~1/3 the size of the long-end lift on the same 96 dates.
findings.why_not_tautology: The tenor contrast is the argument: any confound running through 'volatile macro period' or 'equity selloff' would move all three tenors together, since a risk-off shock repriced the whole curve in this sample. That the front end is nearly flat while 10s and 30s carry the effect points at duration/term-premium specifically. HONEST WEAKNESS: 2Y and 10Y 5d changes are highly correlated, this is one of ~140 comparisons, and the 2Y-vs-30Y gap (31.2% vs 33.3% on n=96) is roughly 2 dates wide — it is a difference in LIFT (1.18 vs 1.57) driven mostly by the differing panel base rates (26.5% vs 21.2%), not by a large gap in raw incidence. Treat the tenor story as a hypothesis this data is consistent with, not one it establishes. With no event calendar I cannot check whether the long-end moves were auction/supply or CPI-driven.

findings.claim: There is NO yield signature across the oracle holding period — the 10Y is a coin flip over the exact windows in which the market rallied 4% at the median.
findings.stat: Sell-date minus buy-date change, trade level n=176: ust_y10 median -0.5bp, mean -1.1bp, down in exactly 50.0% of trades. ust_y30 median 0.0bp, down 47.2%. ust_y2 median 0.0bp, down 40.3%. curve_2s10s median 0.0bp, down 42.6%. By contrast the risk assets move as arithmetic requires: HYG rose in 93.8% of holds, TLT in 63.1%, DXY fell in 57.4%, gold rose in 72.7%.
findings.base_rate: Over all 904 non-null panel dates the 10Y's 5d change is negative 45.1% of the time and its median is +1.0bp; over a matched ~5-trading-day random window the null expectation for 'yield fell' is ~45-50%. The observed 50.0% across oracle holds is indistinguishable from that null.
findings.lift: 1.00x (50.0% vs ~45-50% null) — a zero, and a precisely measured one at n=176.
findings.why_not_tautology: This is a null over the most heavily outcome-selected windows in the dataset — the 176 windows chosen precisely BECAUSE the market rallied hardest in them. Selection has maximum power here to manufacture a rate narrative and it produced exactly nothing. The HYG 93.8% figure in the same table is the control that proves the test has power: where a mechanical co-move exists, this measurement finds it screaming. So 'the best 176 rally windows of 2023-2026 had no yield signature' is a real, non-tautological negative and it directly contradicts the standard 'lower yields drove the rally' narrative for this sample. Caveat: the Treasury par curve is forward-filled to the last business day per the brief, which adds noise to short holds; 23 of 176 trades are same-day (hold=0) and contribute a mechanical zero change to all four rate columns — excluding them, 10Y down-rate is 50.3% of 153, unchanged.

findings.claim: Yield LEVELS and curve SLOPE at oracle buys are pure calendar artifacts — within any single year, oracle buys sit within 7bp of the median day on every tenor and both curve measures.
findings.stat: Pooled, 2s10s median at buys is -12.5bp vs +10.0bp panel — a 22.5bp gap that looks like 'oracle buys happen when the curve is inverted'. Split by year it evaporates. Buy-median minus panel-median, 2s10s: 2023 +5.0bp, 2024 -5.0bp, 2025 -2.0bp, 2026 +2.0bp. 2s30s: +6.0 / -8.5 / -2.0 / 0.0bp. ust_y10: -1.0 / +6.0 / 0.0 / +2.0bp. ust_y2: -7.0 / +5.0 / +6.0 / +0.5bp. Signs alternate; every gap is inside normal daily noise (panel |10Y 5d change| averages 10.2bp).
findings.base_rate: Panel median 2s10s by year: 2023 -64.5bp, 2024 -24.0bp, 2025 +52.0bp, 2026 +50.5bp (n=250/252/250/158). The curve dis-inverted across the sample, so the pooled panel median (+10.0bp) and the pooled buy median (-12.5bp) differ only because trades are not uniformly distributed across a 3.5-year trend.
findings.lift: ~1.00x within every year. The apparent pooled 22.5bp effect is 100% attributable to Simpson's-paradox mixing across a non-stationary trend.
findings.why_not_tautology: Not a tautology, a null — and specifically a warning about the most common way a macro-level backdrop finding gets manufactured. Any level column here (ust_y2/y5/y10/y20/y30, curve_2s10s, curve_2s30s, dxy, tlt, hyg, gold, wti) trends hard over the window, so pooled buy-vs-panel comparisons on levels measure only when trades happened, never what conditions they happened in. All 11 level columns behave this way. The rule this implies: in this dataset, only the *_chg5d columns and within-year comparisons of levels are interpretable at all.

dead_ends: DXY — no signal at buys in either direction. dxy_chg5d > 0 on 57.1% of buy dates vs 50.8% base (lift 1.13, n=98), but the per-year lifts are 1.25 / 0.93 / 1.44 / 0.89 — two years each way, no consistency. The dollar backdrop does not mark oracle lows.

TLT direction — tlt_chg5d < 0 on 60.2% of buys vs 53.4% base (lift 1.13, n=98) and 2023 points the wrong way (0.86). TLT is a duration proxy, so this is the same information as ust_y10_chg5d, which is itself a null (finding 2); the small pooled lift is a restatement of the long-end magnitude effect leaking through, not an independent signal.

GOLD — gold_chg5d < 0 on 50.0% of buys vs 39.2% base (lift 1.27, n=98) looks moderate, but gold's base rate swings wildly by year (43.6% / 38.5% / 26.8% / 53.2%) because gold trended violently in 2025. Per-year lifts 1.06 / 1.34 / 1.64 / 1.21. I did not attempt to decontaminate this against equity drawdown because the base-rate instability makes any pooled number uninterpretable, and I do not have a mechanism that would survive rule 3. Reported as untested rather than as a finding.

WTI — wti_chg5d < 0 on 61.2% of buys vs 51.5% base (lift 1.19, n=98), but 2026 inverts to 0.66. Oil is a risk asset co-moving with equities, so this is the same class of tautology as HYG and I did not promote it; the equity-conditioned test that killed HYG would very likely kill this too, and I did not run it.

CREDIT LEADING EQUITIES — I tested whether HYG turns before the oracle low (residual analysis, orthogonalised HYG 5d move at buys 53.1% negative vs 50.9% base, n=98). There is no lead. Credit is coincident with equities in this sample at the 5-day horizon. A 1-day HYG change would be a better test of lead/lag and is not in the feature set, though it is reconstructible from the hyg level series — I did not build it.

SAME-DAY TRADES AS AN ARTIFACT — I checked whether the rate-shock finding is driven by the 23 hold=0 round trips flagged in the brief. It is not: shock rate 39.1% for same-day trades (n=23) vs 40.4% for multi-day (n=151). No adjustment needed.

finds.lens: VOLATILITY — B_vix, B_vix_chg5d, B_vix_pctile_252d, B_atr14_pct, B_realvol20_ann_pct, B_vol_vs_20d at buys vs sells, against the daily_panel denominator (1,817 rows = 907 SPX + 910 NDX symbol-days; VIX is shared across the two symbols so every calendar day is counted twice — the denominator is symbol-days, matched to the 176 symbol-trades). ~115 distinct cuts/tests across the 6 named columns plus 4 derived measures (VIX minus realised-vol spread, price-orthogonalised VIX residual, within-sym-month percentile rank, forward 5-day low-to-max-high opportunity). Nothing dropped except where stated: vol_vs_20d is null on 1 daily row and 1 buy row; the forward-return panel drops the last 5 bars of each symbol (10 of 1,817 rows). All 44 months x 2 indices used. Scripts: /home/user/INMA-/research-vault/backtest/scratch/vol1.py through vol7.py

findings.claim: The VIX signature at oracle buys is a full price tautology: within its own calendar month the oracle buy sits at VIX rank 0.758, but the month's lowest-low day — selected on price alone with VIX never consulted — sits HIGHER, at 0.857.
findings.stat: Within-sym-month percentile rank of the buy date's VIX: mean 0.758, median 0.833, n=176, +13.7 SE above the 0.500 uniform null. Pure-price null (the single lowest-low day of each of the 88 sym-months): 0.857. Same pattern on vix_pctile_252d (oracle 0.748 vs price-null 0.831) and vix_chg5d (0.661 vs 0.724). Jan-2023 to Aug-2026.
findings.base_rate: Uniform within-month null = 0.500 by construction. Unconditional daily_panel analogue: VIX mean 17.42 / median 16.70 (n=1,817) versus 19.34 / 18.36 at oracle buys.
findings.lift: Buy VIX rank 0.758 vs null 0.500 = +0.258; but versus the price-only null of 0.857 the lift is NEGATIVE (−0.099).
findings.why_not_tautology: It IS the tautology, and that is the finding. VIX is mechanically anti-correlated with index price (daily corr(ret_5d_pct, vix_chg5d) = −0.647, slope −1.04 VIX points per 1% move, n=1,817), so 'oracle buys happen at high VIX' carries no information beyond 'oracle buys happen at price lows'. The decisive number is that a VIX-blind price rule lands on a MORE VIX-extreme day than the oracle does. What would separate them: a volatility measure orthogonal to contemporaneous index return by construction — VIX term-structure slope, VVIX, or skew. None are in this dataset.

findings.claim: Stratifying on the 5-day price return destroys roughly 85% of every VIX lift — the volatility lens survives only as a price restatement, not as an independent marker.
findings.stat: vix_chg5d>+3: raw buy lift 2.70x, within-ret_5d_pct-decile lift 1.29x (56 observed vs 43.5 expected). vix>20: 1.82x to 1.13x (59 obs vs 52.1 exp). vix_pctile_252d>80: 2.02x to 1.23x (60 obs vs 48.9 exp). atr14_pct>1.5: 1.14x to 0.94x (60 obs vs 63.6 exp). Orthogonalised residual (vix_chg5d minus its linear fit on ret_5d_pct; daily residual sd 2.876): buys +0.445 = +0.15 sd, median −0.258.
findings.lift: Raw 2.70x / 2.02x / 1.82x collapses to 1.29x / 1.23x / 1.13x once 5-day return is held fixed. Residual VIX shock at buys = +0.15 standard deviations.
findings.why_not_tautology: A small residual does survive (1.13-1.29x, plus a +0.058 = 3.5 SE within-month VIX-rank residual after controlling for within-month close rank), so VIX is not 100% redundant with price. But the surviving effect is one-fifth of the headline and sits at the magnitude that 115 tested cuts generate by chance. Report the collapse, not the remainder.

findings.claim: Which VIX transform is 'more informative' flips with the denominator: against all days the 5-day CHANGE wins decisively; against the design-matched within-month denominator the LEVEL wins.
findings.stat: All-days denominator at matched base rates: vix_chg5d>+2 (base 19.1%) hits 40.3% of buys, 2.11x; vix>20 (base 18.4%) hits 33.5%, 1.82x. At ~11% base: vix_chg5d>+3 (11.8%) hits 31.8%, 2.70x vs vix>22 (10.0%) hits 18.8%, 1.87x. Tail: vix_chg5d>+5 (5.2%) hits 18.2%, 3.51x vs vix>25 (4.5%) hits 9.7%, 2.14x. Within-sym-month rank of the buy date: vix 0.758 (13.7 SE) vs vix_chg5d 0.661 (7.3 SE).
findings.lift: Change beats level 3.51x vs 2.14x in the tail against all days; level beats change +0.258 vs +0.161 in within-month rank deviation.
findings.why_not_tautology: The flip has a structural cause that must be stated: the oracle takes exactly 2 buys per calendar month per index regardless of regime, so any slow, month-persistent variable (VIX level, ATR, realised vol) is mechanically prevented from concentrating against the all-days denominator, while a fast variable (vix_chg5d) can. Removing the month fixed effect via within-month ranks reverses the ordering. Neither ordering is an edge — both fail the price-stratification test in finding 2. Quoting the all-days lift alone would be a denominator artefact.

findings.claim: Realised volatility is a complete dead end at oracle buys while implied volatility is not — same construct, opposite result — so the marker is a same-day fear spike, not a volatility regime.
findings.stat: Within-sym-month rank at buys: realvol20_ann_pct 0.502 (+0.1 SE from the 0.500 null), atr14_pct 0.569 (+3.1 SE), versus vix 0.758 (+13.7 SE). All-days cuts: realvol20>18 base 25.5% to buys 25.6% (lift 1.00x, k=45); realvol20>22 base 10.0% to 10.2% (1.02x); realvol20>25 base 5.8% to 4.5% (0.79x, k=8); atr14_pct>1.5 base 29.8% to 34.1% (1.14x); atr14_pct>2.0 base 8.5% to 9.7% (1.13x).
findings.base_rate: daily_panel n=1,817: realvol20_ann_pct mean 15.78 / median 14.33 (buys 15.88 / 14.82); atr14_pct mean 1.37 / median 1.26 (buys 1.42 / 1.29).
findings.lift: 1.00x for realvol20>18 — exactly the base rate. 1.13-1.14x for ATR. Against 1.82-2.14x for the VIX level over the identical window.
findings.why_not_tautology: This is a null result, and selection-on-outcome inflates apparent effects rather than erasing them, so the bias cannot manufacture it. The mechanism is legible: realvol20 and ATR14 are backward-looking 14-20 day averages that barely move inside one calendar month and therefore cannot mark a specific day; VIX is a same-day print. Directly usable consequence: 'buy when volatility is elevated' measured on trailing realised vol has zero discriminating power here, and the entire VIX result is a one-day-resolution phenomenon.

findings.claim: The exit signature is not the mirror of the entry — it is about three times fainter, and the oracle sells BEFORE volatility normalises rather than into calm.
findings.stat: Within-sym-month rank deviation from 0.500: buys +0.258 on VIX (13.7 SE) versus sells −0.083 (−3.6 SE), a 3.1x asymmetry. Absolute levels: sell-date VIX mean 17.01 / median 16.36 versus daily 17.42 / 16.70; P(VIX>25) at sells = 4.5% (k=8) against a 4.5% base rate, lift 1.01x. Sell-date within-month VIX rank 0.417 versus 0.273 for the month's highest-high day (the price-only exit null). Best sell-side cut in the whole lens: vix_chg5d<−1, base 32.5% to 42.6% of sells, 1.31x, k=75.
findings.base_rate: daily_panel n=1,817: VIX mean 17.42, P(vix>25)=4.5%, P(vix_chg5d<−1)=32.5%, P(vix_pctile_252d<10)=21.5%, vix_pctile_252d mean 43.30.
findings.lift: 1.01x at sells for VIX>25 — indistinguishable from a random day. 1.31x for the best sell cut against 3.51x for the best buy cut. Entry/exit rank-deviation ratio 0.258 / 0.083 = 3.1x.
findings.why_not_tautology: Selection guarantees a rally precedes every sell, and rallies mechanically depress VIX, so the naive prediction is a strong low-VIX signature at sells. The finding is that this prediction FAILS: sells sit at 17.01 VIX against a 17.42 all-day mean, and their within-month VIX rank (0.417) is far above the price-only exit null (0.273). The oracle exits while the month's volatility is still above its eventual floor. The selection bias argues against this result rather than producing it. What would strengthen it: the forward VIX path after each sell date — computable from this panel, not run.

findings.claim: The only price-orthogonal signal in the whole volatility lens is vol_vs_20d (relative VOLUME, not volatility), and it is symmetric — elevated at both entries and exits, and stronger at exits.
findings.stat: After controlling for within-month close rank: buy residual +0.059 (2.8 SE, n=175), sell residual +0.104 (4.9 SE, n=176). The within-month close-rank profile of volume rank is nearly flat across price deciles (0.61, 0.49, 0.49, 0.49, 0.53, 0.50, 0.51, 0.45, 0.44, 0.50), so it is not a price restatement. All-days cuts: vol_vs_20d>1.1 base 19.3% to buys 34.3% (1.78x, k=60) and sells 31.8% (1.65x, k=56). Every other lens variable has a monotone price-rank profile and a residual between −0.037 and +0.058.
findings.lift: 1.78x at buys and 1.65x at sells for vol_vs_20d>1.1 — the only near-symmetric lift in the lens. Price-controlled residual +0.059 buy / +0.104 sell on a 0-1 rank scale.
findings.why_not_tautology: Volume and |return| co-move and oracle dates are extreme-price days, so some of this is selection. The control is explicit: daily corr(vol_vs_20d, |ret_1d_pct|) is only 0.201 (n=1,816), and after regressing it out the buy and sell residuals are +0.0395 and +0.0386 — both about +0.23 sd, small but present and near-identical. With the flat price-rank profile, the reading is that turning points in BOTH directions land on above-median-volume days independently of the size of that day's move. Two caveats stated plainly: this column is volume, not volatility, and the effect size is modest enough to be a credible member of the 115-cut multiple-comparison pool.

findings.claim: High VIX does not mark a better entry — it doubles the size of the swing available to any entry, a scaling fact measured on ALL days with no selection whatsoever.
findings.stat: Forward low-to-max-high over the next 5 sessions, full daily panel (1,807 of 1,817 rows; last 5 bars per symbol have no window): all days 2.54%; vix>20 3.91% (x1.54, n=334); vix>25 5.17% (x2.04, n=82); atr14_pct>2.0 4.63% (x1.82, n=155); vix_chg5d>+5 4.55% (x1.79, n=94). Forward 5-day close return: all days +0.48% with P(up) 61.3%; vix>25 +2.02% with P(up) 64.6%. This explains the oracle's own return gradient: mean trade return 3.98% for B_vix<15 (n=32) rising monotonically to 8.20% for B_vix>25 (n=17).
findings.base_rate: daily_panel, all days, no conditioning: forward 5-day low-to-max-high = 2.54%; forward 5-day close return +0.48%; P(up) 61.3% (n=1,807).
findings.lift: x2.04 on swing size at VIX>25; only +1.54pp of mean return and +3.3pp of P(up) directionally — the range effect is roughly 4x the directional effect.
findings.why_not_tautology: The denominator is every day in the panel with no conditioning on outcome, so the oracle's selection bias cannot reach it. The real limits are different: (a) the VIX>25 sample is 82 symbol-days but only 15 contiguous SPX episodes spanning 9 of 44 months — effective n is episodes, not days (VIX>20: 37 episodes; vix_chg5d>+5: 27 episodes); (b) Jan-2023 to Aug-2026 was a bull run with mean-reverting vol, so the directional component is regime-flattered; (c) a wider range raises the achievable loss as much as the achievable gain — only a perfect-foresight operator captures the upper half. As a rule this would be 'size positions by realised opportunity, do not treat VIX as a timing signal'; the out-of-sample test is the same low-to-max-high measure on a pre-2023 or post-Aug-2026 window, split by VIX bucket. IT HAS NOT BEEN RUN.

findings.claim: vix_pctile_252d earns its keep only against the all-days denominator and adds essentially nothing over the raw VIX print once the month fixed effect is removed.
findings.stat: Within-sym-month rank of the buy date: vix_pctile_252d 0.748 versus vix 0.758 — the percentile is marginally WORSE. Against all days at matched base rates it is marginally better: vix_pctile>80 (base 16.8%) hits 34.1% of buys, 2.02x, k=60, against vix>20 (base 18.4%) hits 33.5%, 1.82x, k=59 — a one-trade difference. Pushing further out kills it: vix_pctile>90 (base 10.0%) hits 16.5%, lift falls to 1.65x, k=29.
findings.base_rate: daily_panel n=1,817: vix_pctile_252d mean 43.30, median 39.70; P(>80)=16.8%, P(>90)=10.0%, P(>75)=21.5%, P(<20)=32.9%. The measure is left-skewed and NOT uniform — the top decile happens to be 10% of days, but the top quartile is 21.5%, not 25%.
findings.lift: 2.02x vs 1.82x at matched base rate — a 60-vs-59-trade gap, i.e. noise. Non-monotone: the lift DROPS to 1.65x at the >90 cut where a real threshold effect should strengthen.
findings.why_not_tautology: Both measures inherit the price tautology of finding 1, the apparent advantage is one trade out of 176, and it reverses at the more extreme cut. Inside a single calendar month a 252-day trailing percentile is a near-monotone transform of the raw level, so it cannot carry independent information at daily resolution. Recorded to close the question: do not report 'VIX percentile beats VIX level' from this data.

dead_ends: realvol20_ann_pct — the flattest column in the lens. Within-month rank at buys 0.502 (+0.1 SE); realvol20>18 hits 25.6% of buys against a 25.5% base rate (lift 1.00x); realvol20>25 is anti-signal (0.79x, k=8). Trailing realised volatility does not mark oracle entries at all.

atr14_pct — near-dead. Within-month rank 0.569 at buys, and after controlling for within-month close rank the residual is −0.006 (−0.3 SE). Its raw 1.13-1.14x lifts vanish entirely under 5-day-return stratification (0.94x).

VIX minus realised vol (variance-risk-premium proxy, built to test whether implied-over-realised was the true marker). Buys sit 1.8 points above the daily mean (3.46 vs 1.64), but the tail cut vrp>6 gives only 1.59x (base 19.6% to 31.2%) — weaker than the raw VIX level cut — and it is driven entirely by the VIX numerator since realvol contributes nothing. No independent variance-premium effect. At sells the vrp lift is 0.87-1.00x, i.e. nothing.

Low VIX percentile as a SELL marker. vix_pctile_252d<10: base 21.5% to 26.7% of sells (1.24x, k=47); <20: base 32.9% to 36.9% (1.12x). The oracle does not exit into calm — the strongest version of this hypothesis yields 1.24x, inside the multiple-comparison noise floor for 115 cuts.

Oracle trade RETURN versus B_vix_chg5d bucket — non-monotone and uninterpretable: chg5d<−2 gives 5.15% mean (n=23), 0-to-+2 gives 4.00% (n=43), >+5 gives 6.44% (n=32). Both tails beat the middle. No usable gradient, in contrast to the clean monotone gradient on VIX LEVEL (3.98% to 8.20%).

Same-day (hold=0) round trips as a confound I chased and had to partly concede: the 23 same-day trades are disproportionately high-vol (mean B_vix 21.13 vs 19.34 overall; mean B_vix_chg5d 4.17 vs 2.10), because a high-vol day has a wide intraday low-to-high range by construction. Excluding all 23 shrinks the headline VIX-shock lifts from 2.70x to 2.33x (chg5d>+3) and 3.51x to 3.03x (chg5d>+5) on n=153. Real contamination, but it accounts for only about a seventh of the effect — not the explanation.

finds.lens: TRADE ANATOMY — hold-length and return distributions, leg1→leg2 handoff structure, month-level totals vs realised range/vol, SPX-vs-NDX, concentration of the oracle's edge over buy&hold, and up- vs down-month capture. All month-level denominators (range, path, realised vol, buy&hold) were rebuilt from daily_panel.csv (1,817 rows) into 88 (sym, month) cells; nothing was dropped — all 176 trades, all 44 months, both indices are in every number below. Scripts: /home/user/INMA-/research-vault/backtest/scratch/anat.py … anat6.py.

findings.claim: The oracle's monthly return is almost entirely a restatement of that month's high-low range: oracle_total = 0.91 + 1.166 x range_pct, R^2 = 0.773, and the capture ratio oracle_total/range is tight at 1.33 with CV 19.8%.
findings.stat: n=88 (sym,month) cells, Jan-2023..Aug-2026. Pearson r(oracle_total, month range) = +0.879 (R^2 0.773); vs realised vol r=+0.835, ATR% r=+0.800, path (sum |daily ret|) r=+0.775, VIX level r=+0.566 (Spearman only +0.260). Capture = oracle/range: mean 1.327, median 1.359, sd 0.262, min 0.570, max 1.821. Stable across years (2023 1.259, 2024 1.376, 2025 1.363, 2026 1.305) and indices (spx 1.342, ndx 1.313). NOT scale-free: falls monotonically across range quartiles 1.508 / 1.385 / 1.275 / 1.141.
findings.base_rate: From daily_panel.csv the 88 month-cells have high-low range mean 7.47%, median 6.79%; realised vol (realvol20_ann_pct) mean 14.6. Buy&hold per month-cell: mean +1.96%, 30/88 negative.
findings.lift: Oracle mean 9.62%/month-cell = 1.33x the month's realised range and 4.9x buy&hold's 1.96%. Range alone explains 77% of cross-sectional variance in oracle return; VIX explains ~32% and adds nothing over range.
findings.why_not_tautology: Mostly tautological by construction - an algorithm maximising low-to-high pairs must scale with the low-to-high range. What is NOT tautological is (a) the multiplier sits reliably ABOVE 1.0 (mean 1.33), which is only possible because the second leg re-uses a down-leg the range does not contain, and (b) the tightness: CV 19.8% with the same mean in every year and both indices, i.e. the month's realised range is a near-sufficient statistic for the whole oracle. Separating the two would require an EX-ANTE range forecast: replace realised range with a forecast (VIX, prior-month ATR) and re-fit out of sample. THAT TEST HAS NOT BEEN RUN, and the weak VIX rank correlation (0.26) warns the ex-ante version will be much weaker. This is a description, not a strategy.

findings.claim: The second leg is worth ~47% on top of the single best trade available in the month - the oracle's advantage over a one-shot perfect trade is large and universal, never absent in any month.
findings.stat: Best single low->high pair inside each calendar month, recomputed directly from daily_panel highs/lows: mean 6.54%, median 5.73% (n=88). Oracle 2-leg total: mean 9.62%, median 8.59%. Marginal value of leg 2: mean +3.08pp, median +2.78pp = +47% uplift. 0 of 88 months where leg 2 adds less than 1pp; 43% of months where it adds more than 3pp. Leg1 and leg2 contribute almost equally (leg1 sum 413.0%, mean 4.69%; leg2 sum 433.7%, mean 4.93%; leg2 > leg1 in 53% of months), with identical median hold (5.0 days each).
findings.base_rate: The best-single-leg figure IS the panel-derived denominator: in 56 of 88 cells it equals the full month high-low range exactly (month low precedes month high); in the other 32 it is strictly less. Month range mean 7.47%, buy&hold mean 1.96%.
findings.lift: 9.62% vs 6.54% best-single = +3.08pp, x1.47. Versus buy&hold's 1.96%, best-single alone is already x3.3 and the second leg takes it to x4.9.
findings.why_not_tautology: Both quantities are oracle-optimal, so selection-on-outcome inflates numerator and denominator equally and largely cancels - the ratio is a structural property of the price path (how often a month contains a second separable drawdown-and-recovery). Residual bias: the 2-leg optimum is >= the 1-leg optimum by construction. The informative part is the SIZE (47%, never below 1pp in 88 months), which says these months genuinely contain two V-shapes, not one.

findings.claim: The oracle's return is NOT concentrated in a few months - it is spread more evenly than the month-range distribution itself and far more evenly than buy&hold; there is no losing month in 88. The EDGE over buy&hold is moderately lumpier, and April 2025 alone is 8.5% of it.
findings.stat: n=88 cells. Oracle total: top 8/88 = 18.6% of the 846.7% sum (uniform 9.1%); top 4 = 11.3%; top 22 = 38.7%. Gini 0.210 vs month-range Gini 0.223 and buy&hold Gini 0.241. Minimum cell +4.02% (spx 2026-07); 88/88 positive. Edge (oracle - buy&hold): mean 7.66%, median 6.61%, min 1.71%, max 30.12%, Gini 0.318, top 8/88 = 22.2% of the 673.9pp total edge. Largest single driver April 2025 (ndx +30.1pp, spx +26.9pp = 8.5% of all edge): range 19.8%/17.8%, realvol 51.5/42.0, mean VIX 32.0, buy&hold +0.85%/-0.76% - a complete crash-and-recover round trip inside one month.
findings.base_rate: Buy&hold over the same 88 cells: top 8 months = 47.2% of the summed 172.8%, 30/88 negative, Gini 0.241.
findings.lift: Top-8 concentration 18.6% (oracle) vs 47.2% (buy&hold) - the oracle is 2.5x less top-heavy. Worst-month floor +4.02% vs buy&hold's 30 negative months.
findings.why_not_tautology: 'Every month positive' is pure tautology - the optimiser cannot pick a loser. The DEGREE of evenness is not forced: an oracle dominated by two crash months was entirely possible and is not what happened. The Gini comparison uses panel-derived denominators and shows the oracle's distribution is essentially the range distribution rescaled (0.210 vs 0.223), while buy&hold is lumpier because trend concentrates in a few months and range does not.
